### 6.3.4 Doctrinal Legal Construction and the Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

Confronting the destructive complexity of affective persuasion systems and AI-based psychographic data extraction, Indonesia’s legal doctrinal framework must undergo radical reconstruction through a profound interdisciplinary reading that synthesizes Civil Law, cyber criminal law, and modern cognitive psychology (Kahneman & Tversky, 2011). We can no longer rely exclusively on classical contract law doctrines grounded in the liberal concept of *informed consent*—a framework that posits users as rational, autonomous economic actors capable of reading, comprehending, and analyzing 50-page Terms of Service agreements within a three-second window before clicking "Agree" (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). In the era of generative artificial intelligence, such legal fiction ceases to be a form of protection and instead becomes a legitimate instrument of legal oppression (Zuboff, 2019). Consequently, Indonesia’s positive Civil Law doctrine, particularly the provisions regarding Defects of Will / Vitiated Consent found in Article 1321 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek)—which encompasses Mistake / Error (*dwaling*), Fraud / Deceit (*bedrog*), and Duress (*dwang*), as well as its extension into the realms of psychological *misrepresentation* and Undue Influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*)—must be organically integrated into the juridical interpretation of Article 20 of the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) (see also Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code).

The reconstruction of individual sovereignty in the digital era demands that all forms of deep psychographic data processing and the application of subliminal manipulation techniques by AI systems be legally categorized as high-risk processing that *ipso facto* violates the principle of substantive justice (Calo, 2014). If artificial intelligence service providers employ covert emotional manipulation or the illusion of artificial intimacy to coerce or deceive data subjects into surrendering their personal data rights, the resulting consent must be declared legally void, as it was obtained through high-level *cognitive fraud* (Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code). Furthermore, national legal instruments must adopt progressive principles such as *algorithmic transparency* and the *right to human intervention*, aligning with the spirit of Articles 5 and 50 of the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). Every Indonesian citizen interacting with intelligent systems must possess the absolute right to refuse emotional profiling by machines, as well as the constitutional right to receive comprehensible explanations (*explainable AI*) regarding how algorithmic decisions or recommendations are generated and how they impact their psychological and social well-being (Floridi, 2013).

In closing this extensive discourse, the digital sovereignty of the Republic of Indonesia amidst the storm of the artificial intelligence revolution can never be realized solely through the construction of domestic physical server infrastructure or the issuance of ceremonial ISO data compliance certifications (Pradani, 2023). True sovereignty demands the political courage and intellectual acuity of the state to defend the cognitive space of its citizens against a global algorithmic imperialism that intrudes, without permission, into the most private recesses of human consciousness (Wiener, 1950). The Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27 of 2022) must be enforced with high moral resolve and analytical precision to ensure that the mental vault and inner sanctum of every Indonesian citizen remain a sovereign territory, untouched by the cold, data-hungry, and control-seeking hands of binary code (Jonas, 1979; Levinas, 1961).

# Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty in the Digital Era: Harmonizing National Regulation with Global Ethical Standards

By: **Ilham Pradani**

---

The reconstruction of individual sovereignty in the digital era demands that all forms of deep psychographic data processing and the application of subliminal manipulation techniques by AI systems be legally categorized as high-risk processing that *ipso facto* violates the principle of substantive justice. If artificial intelligence service providers employ covert emotional manipulation or the illusion of artificial intimacy to coerce or deceive data subjects into surrendering their personal data rights, the international and domestic legal frameworks face an acute crisis of legitimacy.

The following section elaborates on a deep discourse regarding how national legal frameworks must be aligned with global ethical standards to shield the Cognitive Liberty of citizens from the exploitation inherent in transnational platform capitalism.
